sm: The speaker says social media and the flood of competing ideologies make life feel complicated and spike his stress, but he argues life is really simple. He points to Psalm 73, asking who he has in heaven but God, and reads it as saying that on earth you are utterly alone. He connects this to Augustine groping in the dark until he finds rest in God, and to Herman Bavinck's line that man is an enigma whose only solution is God. Leaning on creatures, he says, makes them snap under the weight of the soul. He recalls standing before a beautiful waterfall, pressured by John Piper-style teaching to be constantly delighting in God, and finding he simply could not, so eventually he stopped trying.

Here he reflects on Paul's words that the sting of death is sin, and suggests life has a sting too, which is also sin. As we age and approach death, guilt and shame can drive how we think, love and choose. He lists things that make life sting: seeing corrupt people prosper, natural disasters that destroy a lifetime of work and make life feel vain, and personal failure. He adds a middle category, where tragedies are made worse by the haunting question of how much responsibility we bear. Those questions often go unanswered even at the end of life. Switching from one ideology or tribe to another, he says, is just chasing the wind, so he asks what we are to do about the sting of life.

He asks who can remove the sting of life, mentioning sudden panic attacks and even a hypothetical perfect person tormented in the wilderness. Repeating that, according to Psalm 73, you are utterly alone, he says we are the villains we fear we might be, and that even a small fraction of failure would deserve hell. Life is complicated mainly because we refuse this simple truth and invent ideologies to explain it away. The simple solution is faith in God. He notes that the word confidence comes from the Latin for with faith, so the truly confident person has repented and believed in Jesus. Such a person sees blessings as undeserved gifts and afflictions as no longer punishment, because Christ took the punishment at the cross.

He continues that Christ removed the sting of death and therefore of life, so believers are not truly alone, since Jesus felt the loneliness and agony of death and hell. He cites C. S. Lewis on friendship, saying Jesus is an older brother who says you too, I am with you in this. He notes that the verse from Psalm 73 forms the two halves of George Swinnick's book The Fading of the Flesh and the Flourishing of Faith, which personifies death as a screech owl. Outside Jesus there is no way to remove life's sting, though in Christ tragedies become only tragedies, no longer worsened by guilt. He quotes First John on having confidence when Christ appears, and closes by urging listeners to repent, return to Jesus, and live.
